mainText:
If you only remember one thing: today is election day, and data centers are on the ballot.

Section one. Data centers hit the ballot. From your Rundown newsletter. About twenty communities across the U S are voting today on banning or pausing data centers. Democrats are projected to flip the House, which could end two years of easy treatment for A I companies close to the White House. Some Democrats want a federal freeze on new data centers. Meanwhile, Open A I is reportedly planning to rebrand them as "A I compute campuses," and to push state bills that give locals a voice. Why it matters: A I has a public image problem, and a new name won't fix local anger.

Section two. China's chips and models. From your China A I weekly digest. C X M T, China's memory chip maker, reported third quarter revenue up over six hundred percent from a year ago. It is also sampling advanced H B M three E memory, but reported yields are only twenty to thirty percent. Robot maker Unitree grew revenue about seventy percent, while tripling down on research. And Moonshot launched Kimi K three point one Pro, with open weights promised by November fourth, after apologizing for a rocky rollout. Why it matters: China is closing gaps in memory and open models, even with export controls in place.

Section three. A I policy in Europe. From your A I Act newsletter, a conversation with a journalist about how reporters uncover what is really happening with the European A I Act. Why it matters: how the rules get enforced will depend on reporting like this.

Also in your Reads: The New Yorker has a piece on how the political right is eyeing the exits, and another on the year math changed forever. Noosphere has election night coverage planned. And a Substack profile of a local reporter who took the government to court twice.

A note: your Readwise saves were not available this morning, so that source is skipped until it's reconnected.

The thread today: A I is leaving the lab and meeting voters, from American ballots to China's factories. Have a good day, Sin.
